name: Interventricular Septum
summary: The muscular and membranous wall separating the ventricles. It carries the bundle branches and contributes actively to the contraction of both ventricles.

anatomy.location: Runs obliquely between the two ventricular cavities, bulging into the right ventricle so that in cross-section the left ventricle appears circular and the right ventricle crescentic.
anatomy.shape: A large inferior muscular portion, thick and continuous with the left ventricular free wall, and a small superior membranous portion beneath the aortic valve. The membranous septum has an atrioventricular part separating the right atrium from the left ventricle, and an interventricular part.
relations: To the left: the left ventricular cavity
To the right: the right ventricular cavity, with the moderator band arising from its lower part
Superiorly: the aortic valve, in continuity with the membranous septum
The bundle of His penetrates the membranous septum and divides on its crest into the bundle branches
attachments: Continuous with the free walls of both ventricles
Membranous portion attached to the aortic annulus and the central fibrous body
Septal papillary muscle and septal chordae of the tricuspid valve on the right side
Moderator band running from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle
anatomy.bloodSupply: The anterior two thirds are supplied by septal perforating branches of the left anterior descending artery; the posterior third is supplied by the posterior descending artery — from the right coronary artery in a right-dominant circulation.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Great and middle cardiac veins draining to the coronary sinus.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac plexus, together with the specialised conduction tissue running within it.
anatomy.function: Contributes contractile force to both ventricles and houses the bundle branches that ensure rapid, coordinated ventricular activation.

physiology.function: Behaves functionally as part of the left ventricle. Septal contraction is essential to normal left ventricular ejection, and its motion is a sensitive indicator of both ischaemia and conduction abnormality.

pressures.label: Transseptal gradient in systole
pressures.value: large — LV about 120 mmHg against RV about 25 mmHg

pressures.label: Hypertrophy threshold
pressures.value: wall thickness of 15 mm or more raises the possibility of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

physiology.electrical: Septal depolarisation is the first event of ventricular activation and proceeds from left to right, producing the small initial q wave in the lateral leads. The right bundle branch, and the left bundle's anterior and posterior fascicles, run subendocardially on either side.
hemodynamics: The large systolic pressure difference across the septum means any defect produces left-to-right shunting
Septal position depends on the relative pressures in the two ventricles — right ventricular pressure or volume overload flattens it, producing the D-shaped left ventricle
Left bundle branch block causes septal activation delay and dyssynchronous contraction, the substrate targeted by cardiac resynchronisation therapy

pathology.name: Ventricular septal defect
pathology.note: The commonest congenital cardiac defect at birth; most occur in the membranous portion and cause left-to-right shunting.

pathology.name: Post-infarction ventricular septal rupture
pathology.note: A mechanical complication typically occurring days after a large infarct, causing acute shunt and cardiogenic shock.

pathology.name: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy
pathology.note: Characteristic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; may cause dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

pathology.name: Bundle branch block
pathology.note: Conduction disease within the septum delays activation of one ventricle and widens the QRS complex.

clinical.relevance: The septum is where anatomy, conduction and ischaemia intersect: it carries the bundle branches, it is the site of the commonest congenital defect, and its thickness and motion inform the diagnosis of cardiomyopathy and coronary disease.
examination: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a thrill in a ventricular septal defect
Ejection systolic murmur that increases on Valsalva in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Wide or paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound in bundle branch block
imaging: Echocardiography for septal thickness, motion and colour Doppler evidence of shunting
Cardiac MRI for septal fibrosis and accurate wall thickness
Left ventriculography and oximetry runs to quantify a shunt
ECG for bundle branch block and septal q waves
procedures: Surgical or transcatheter closure of ventricular septal defects
Alcohol septal ablation or surgical septal myectomy in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Endomyocardial biopsy from the right side of the septum
His-bundle and left bundle branch area pacing

keyPoints: Large muscular portion plus a small membranous portion beneath the aortic valve.
Carries the bundle of His and both bundle branches.
Anterior two thirds supplied by LAD septal perforators; posterior third by the posterior descending artery.
Septal depolarisation goes left to right, producing normal septal q waves laterally.
Ventricular septal defect is the commonest congenital cardiac defect at birth.

name: Interatrial Septum
summary: The thin wall between the atria. Its central depression, the fossa ovalis, marks the site of the fetal foramen ovale and remains probe-patent in a substantial minority of adults.

anatomy.location: Between the right and left atria, oriented obliquely so that the right atrium lies anterior and to the right of the left atrium.
anatomy.shape: Thin and largely fibromuscular. Its most prominent feature on the right atrial side is the fossa ovalis, a shallow oval depression bounded superiorly and anteriorly by the limbus. The true septum is confined largely to the floor of the fossa; much of the surrounding 'septum' is infolded atrial wall containing extracardiac fat.
relations: Right atrial surface: the fossa ovalis, with the limbus above and the tendon of Todaro below
Left atrial surface: smooth, with the valve of the fossa ovalis
Inferiorly: the triangle of Koch and the AV node
Anteriorly and superiorly: the aortic root indents the septum
attachments: Continuous with the walls of both atria
Contributes to the central fibrous body inferiorly
Limbus fossae ovalis marking the free edge of the embryological septum secundum
anatomy.bloodSupply: Atrial branches of the right coronary and left circumflex arteries, including the AV nodal artery inferiorly.
anatomy.venousDrainage: Thebesian veins of the atrial walls.
anatomy.innervation: Cardiac plexus, with ganglionated plexi nearby.
anatomy.function: Separates the systemic and pulmonary venous returns after birth. In fetal life, the foramen ovale within it allows oxygenated placental blood to bypass the lungs.

physiology.function: Maintains complete separation of the two atria in postnatal life. Its embryological arrangement of overlapping septum primum and septum secundum acts as a one-way flap valve before birth.

pressures.label: Consequence
pressures.value: the small left-to-right gradient means most septal defects shunt left to right

physiology.electrical: Interatrial conduction crosses principally via Bachmann's bundle superiorly; the AV node lies at the inferior margin within the triangle of Koch.
hemodynamics: After birth, the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance and the rise in left atrial pressure press the flap of the foramen ovale closed
In roughly a quarter of adults the flap never fuses, leaving a patent foramen ovale that can open transiently when right atrial pressure rises
A persistent left-to-right shunt causes right atrial and right ventricular volume overload and, over decades, pulmonary vascular disease

pathology.name: Atrial septal defect
pathology.note: Secundum defects at the fossa ovalis are commonest; primum and sinus venosus defects involve different parts of the septum and have distinct associations.

pathology.name: Patent foramen ovale
pathology.note: Present in a substantial minority of adults; implicated in paradoxical embolism and cryptogenic stroke in selected patients.

pathology.name: Atrial septal aneurysm
pathology.note: Redundant, mobile septal tissue, often found alongside a patent foramen ovale.

pathology.name: Eisenmenger syndrome
pathology.note: Long-standing left-to-right shunting raises pulmonary vascular resistance until the shunt reverses and cyanosis develops.

clinical.relevance: The interatrial septum is both a source of pathology and a route of access: transseptal puncture through the fossa ovalis is the standard entry to the left atrium for atrial fibrillation ablation and mitral interventions.
conditions: Patent foramen ovale and cryptogenic stroke
Sinus venosus defect with anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
examination: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound in a significant atrial septal defect
Pulmonary ejection systolic murmur from increased right-sided flow
Tricuspid mid-diastolic flow murmur with a large shunt
Right ventricular heave with volume overload
imaging: Transthoracic echocardiography with agitated saline contrast (bubble study)
Transoesophageal echocardiography for defect size, rims and suitability for device closure
Cardiac MRI or CT for anomalous pulmonary venous connections and shunt quantification
procedures: Transcatheter device closure of secundum defects and selected patent foramina ovale
Surgical patch closure for primum and sinus venosus defects
Transseptal puncture for left atrial access
Atrial septostomy in selected congenital lesions

keyPoints: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale and the target for transseptal puncture.
A patent foramen ovale persists in roughly a quarter of adults and is usually of no consequence.
Secundum defects at the fossa ovalis are the commonest type of atrial septal defect.
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound is the classic auscultatory sign.
The AV node lies at the inferior margin of the septum in the triangle of Koch.
